text: With raw_customers really sitting in Snowflake, it's time to create the dbt project itself. This lesson covers the real dbt init command, where the actual Snowflake connection lives, and how to confirm it works before writing a single model.

dbt init jaffle_shop_capstone scaffolds the project — the same real command from the prerequisite dbt course. It produces dbt_project.yml, naming the project and a profile — just a name, not a connection yet — plus a models folder and a few starter files. Notice profile is set to jaffle_shop_capstone. That string matters in the next step.

The real connection — the actual Snowflake account, warehouse, and credentials — never lives inside the project folder. It lives in profiles.yml, outside the project, by default in a dot-dbt folder in your home directory, so nobody accidentally commits a password to Git. Here's the real syntax: type snowflake, your account, your username, and critically, database set to jaffle_shop_raw — the exact database Lesson 3 loaded raw_customers into. This file is what makes dbt able to see that table at all.

Two files, one shared name. dbt_project.yml gets checked into version control and says profile colon jaffle_shop_capstone. profiles.yml never gets checked in, and its top-level key has to be that exact same string, jaffle_shop_capstone. That shared name is how dbt connects a project to its credentials — two files, two purposes, joined by one name.

Before writing any model, confirm the connection actually works. Run dbt debug. A working connection ends with Connection test, OK connection ok. If it doesn't, dbt debug tells you exactly which setting is wrong — a typo'd account name, an expired key, a role that can't see jaffle_shop_raw. Fixing that here is far cheaper than debugging a confusing model error later that's actually a connection problem in disguise.

With a working connection confirmed, the project is ready for its first real file. Next lesson, we declare raw_customers as an actual dbt source — a real sources.yml, pointing dbt at the table you loaded in Lesson 3.
